summary: Registers a media type for Open eBook Publication Structure package files. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Electronic books come as packages with a table of contents file. This note registers an official label for that file so computers know what it is.

subtitle: Official media type for Open eBook Publication Structure package files

tldr.problem: Electronic books in the Open eBook Publication Structure format required a standardized way to identify their package files (.opf files) when stored on disk, referenced in container files, or transmitted over the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the media type application/oebps-package+xml for OPF files, allowing systems to properly recognize and handle these XML-based eBook package descriptors.
tldr.outcome: The media type was registered with IANA, enabling eBook readers and other applications to correctly identify and process OPF files across different systems.

today: The media type application/oebps-package+xml was registered with IANA and remains the standard way to identify OEBPS package files. OEBPS has since evolved, with IDPF now maintaining the EPUB standard as the successor format for most eBooks.

sections.title: The eBook Package Format
sections.content:
The Open eBook Publication Structure (OEBPS) is a standard for packaging electronic books. Each eBook contains multiple files: the actual book content, stylesheets, images, and a manifest. The OPF file (Open Package Format) is the central XML file that describes the entire publication. It lists all the files that make up the eBook and provides metadata about them—title, author, language, and other descriptive information.

OEBPS is maintained by the International Digital Publishing Forum (IDPF). When OPF files are edited on disk, referenced in container files, or transmitted over networks, systems need a standardized way to identify what type of file they are.
sections.plainLanguage: An eBook is actually a folder full of files. One special file (called OPF) is like a table of contents that says what all the other files are. Computers need to recognize this special file.

sections.title: The Media Type Registration
sections.content:
RFC 4839 registers the media type application/oebps-package+xml for OPF files. The application type indicates it is application-specific data, the oebps-package subtype identifies it as an OEBPS package, and the +xml suffix indicates it is XML. The files are encoded in UTF-8 or UTF-16 XML.

The registration includes the file extension (.opf) and notes the applications that use this media type, including eBook readers from various vendors such as Microsoft Reader, OSoft reader, MobiPocket, and others. The media type is marked as COMMON usage, meaning it is widely used on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The official label for OPF files is 'application/oebps-package+xml'. When a computer sees a .opf file, it knows to treat it as an eBook package description.

sections.title: Parsing and Security
sections.content:
OPF files are well-formed XML documents, so they are subject to all the security considerations of XML. The RFC notes that it is possible to create malicious files containing malformed data, but most XML parsers protect themselves by strictly enforcing XML conformance. Applications processing OPF files should rigorously validate the size and validity of retrieved data.

The OEBPS standard provides no built-in encryption, signing, or authentication mechanisms within the file format itself, so those security features would need to be handled by the application or storage system containing the OPF file.
sections.plainLanguage: Since OPF files are just XML, they can potentially contain harmful code. Programs reading them should be careful to check what is actually in the file.

references.text: "Open eBook Publication Structure 1.2", International Digital Publishing Forum (IDPF), 2002.
